name: Return on Investment
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The One Number Every Quantum Pitch Deck Tries to Skip
lesson.summary: ROI is the simplest lens for judging whether a dollar in quantum computing came back with more dollars attached, and it is the question this entire book keeps returning to.
lesson.body:
Return on investment answers one plain question: did more value come back than went in, and how much more. The formula is Net Gain divided by Cost of Investment, expressed as a percentage, where Net Gain equals Value Returned minus Cost. It is a ratio rather than a raw dollar amount, which is exactly what makes it useful for comparing wildly different scales of spending, a $500,000 quantum pilot and a $5,000,000 cloud migration do not need to be the same size to be judged on the same scale.

Here is a worked example. A mid-size bank spends $2,000,000 on a two-year quantum computing feasibility pilot exploring portfolio optimization, a commonly cited early use case for the technology. By the end, the bank estimates the pilot generated $2,600,000 in value: some from a genuinely faster optimization routine that made it into production, some from recruiting and reputational value as a technology-forward employer, and some from the strategic insight of knowing whether further investment is worthwhile. Net Gain equals $2,600,000 minus $2,000,000, or $600,000. ROI equals $600,000 divided by $2,000,000, which is 0.30, or 30 percent.

That 30 percent figure means little in isolation. ROI only becomes meaningful once compared against alternatives and against time: a 30 percent return earned over two years is a very different result from the same 30 percent earned in two months. This is precisely why ROI is a foundational tool rather than a complete one, and why it opens this book's financial toolkit rather than closing it. On its own, ROI says nothing about when the cash actually arrived, which is what net present value corrects for; nothing about how likely that $2,600,000 estimate was to materialize versus being optimistic marketing, which is what expected value and probability of success address; and nothing about what else that $2,000,000 could have earned instead, which is opportunity cost.

Quantum computing ROI figures deserve unusual scrutiny for a structural reason: much of the "return" side is soft and self-reported rather than hard and auditable. Patents filed, talent attracted, board-level prestige, and options on a future technology are real, but they are not revenue or measured cost savings, and they are far easier to inflate. When a vendor or internal team quotes an ROI figure for a quantum initiative, the first skeptical question should always be: what exactly is in the numerator, and who produced that estimate.

None of this makes ROI a weak tool, quite the opposite. It is the plainest, most falsifiable question you can ask of any investment. Every other concept in this book's financial toolkit, net present value, risk adjustment, expected value, opportunity cost, and the sunk cost trap, is really a refinement of this same question, adjusted for timing, risk, and uncertainty. Keep the simple formula close at hand, because quantum computing's promoters tend to bury it in complexity precisely when a straight ROI calculation would be least flattering to their pitch.
